claim: Familial hemiplegic migraine type 1 (FHM1) is caused by specific missense mutations in CACNA1A that encodes the α1A subunit of neuronal voltage-gated CaV2.1 (P/Q-type) Ca2+ channels.
source: FHM type 1 (FHM1) is caused by specific missense mutations in CACNA1A that encodes the α1A subunit of neuronal voltage-gated CaV2.1 (P/Q-type) Ca2+ channels (Ophoff et al., 1996; Ferrari et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published research (Ophoff et al., 1996; Ferrari et al., 2015).

claim: Patients carrying the R192Q mutation display only hemiplegic migraine.
source: While patients carrying the R192Q mutation display only hemiplegic migraine, those with the S218L mutation show additional clinical features, such as cerebellar ataxia and seizures (Ferrari et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to published research (Ferrari et al., 2015).

claim: Patients with the S218L mutation show additional clinical features, such as cerebellar ataxia and seizures.
source: While patients carrying the R192Q mutation display only hemiplegic migraine, those with the S218L mutation show additional clinical features, such as cerebellar ataxia and seizures (Ferrari et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to published research (Ferrari et al., 2015).

claim: In patients with the S218L mutation, even trivial head trauma was shown to trigger severe, sometimes fatal attacks that are associated with seizures, coma, and massive brain edema.
source: In patients with the S218L mutation, even trivial head trauma was shown to trigger severe, sometimes fatal attacks that are associated with seizures, coma, and massive brain edema (Fitzsimons and Wolfenden, 1985; Ophoff et al., 1996; Kors et al., 2001; Stam et al., 2009; Ferrari et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by multiple citations to published research (Fitzsimons and Wolfenden, 1985; Ophoff et al., 1996; Kors et al., 2001; Stam et al., 2009; Ferrari et al., 2015).

claim: Transgenic knock-in mice expressing the human FHM1 S218L CaV2.1 channel mutation exhibit increased neuronal Ca2+ influx.
source: Experiments performed in transgenic knock-in mice expressing the human FHM1 S218L CaV2.1 channel mutation (van den Maagdenberg et al., 2010) exhibit increased neuronal Ca2+ influx, enhanced cortical glutamatergic synaptic transmission, and an increased susceptibility to experimentally induced cortical spreading depolarizations (CSDs) (Eikermann-Haerter et al., 2009; van den Maagdenberg et al., 2010; Chanda et al., 2013; Ferrari et al., 2015; Vecchia et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published research (van den Maagdenberg et al., 2010; Eikermann-Haerter et al., 2009; Chanda et al., 2013; Ferrari et al., 2015; Vecchia et al., 2015).

claim: Transgenic knock-in mice expressing the human FHM1 S218L CaV2.1 channel mutation exhibit enhanced cortical glutamatergic synaptic transmission.
source: Experiments performed in transgenic knock-in mice expressing the human FHM1 S218L CaV2.1 channel mutation (van den Maagdenberg et al., 2010) exhibit increased neuronal Ca2+ influx, enhanced cortical glutamatergic synaptic transmission, and an increased susceptibility to experimentally induced cortical spreading depolarizations (CSDs) (Eikermann-Haerter et al., 2009; van den Maagdenberg et al., 2010; Chanda et al., 2013; Ferrari et al., 2015; Vecchia et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published research (van den Maagdenberg et al., 2010; Eikermann-Haerter et al., 2009; Chanda et al., 2013; Ferrari et al., 2015; Vecchia et al., 2015).

claim: Transgenic knock-in mice expressing the human FHM1 S218L CaV2.1 channel mutation exhibit an increased susceptibility to experimentally induced cortical spreading depolarizations (CSDs).
source: Experiments performed in transgenic knock-in mice expressing the human FHM1 S218L CaV2.1 channel mutation (van den Maagdenberg et al., 2010) exhibit increased neuronal Ca2+ influx, enhanced cortical glutamatergic synaptic transmission, and an increased susceptibility to experimentally induced cortical spreading depolarizations (CSDs) (Eikermann-Haerter et al., 2009; van den Maagdenberg et al., 2010; Chanda et al., 2013; Ferrari et al., 2015; Vecchia et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published research (van den Maagdenberg et al., 2010; Eikermann-Haerter et al., 2009; Chanda et al., 2013; Ferrari et al., 2015; Vecchia et al., 2015).

claim: CSDs have been implicated in swelling of neuronal cells in healthy brain.
source: Since CSDs have been implicated in swelling of neuronal cells in healthy brain and were suggested to be involved in brain edema formation under pathological conditions (Takano et al., 2007; Seidel et al., 2016; Hartings et al., 2017), we hypothesized that a higher susceptibility to CSDs may result in overshooting edema formation and subsequent worsen outcome after traumatic brain injury (TBI) of FHM1 mutation carriers.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published research (Takano et al., 2007; Seidel et al., 2016; Hartings et al., 2017).

claim: CSDs were suggested to be involved in brain edema formation under pathological conditions.
source: Since CSDs have been implicated in swelling of neuronal cells in healthy brain and were suggested to be involved in brain edema formation under pathological conditions (Takano et al., 2007; Seidel et al., 2016; Hartings et al., 2017), we hypothesized that a higher susceptibility to CSDs may result in overshooting edema formation and subsequent worsen outcome after traumatic brain injury (TBI) of FHM1 mutation carriers.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published research (Takano et al., 2007; Seidel et al., 2016; Hartings et al., 2017).

claim: Brain trauma induces bilateral CSDs.
source: Following TBI, we observed similar changes, that is a depression of the EEG and a negative shift of the DC signal, while CBF increased over both cerebral hemispheres (Figure 1D) indicating that brain trauma, unlike KCl application, induces bilateral CSDs, as previously described (von Baumgarten et al., 2008).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 1D and a citation to published research (von Baumgarten et al., 2008).

claim: Only 2 out of 18 investigated WT mice showed one CSD after removal of the bone flap.
source: While only one CSD was observed in 2/18 investigated WT mice (n = 8 S218L WT littermates and n = 10 R192Q WT littermates) and in 3/10 heterozygous S218L mutant mice, all homozygous FHM1 mutant mice (n = 7 S218L and n = 8 R192Q mutant mice) showed at least one CSD.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from CSD recordings after bone flap removal.

claim: 3 out of 10 heterozygous S218L mutant mice showed one CSD after removal of the bone flap.
source: While only one CSD was observed in 2/18 investigated WT mice (n = 8 S218L WT littermates and n = 10 R192Q WT littermates) and in 3/10 heterozygous S218L mutant mice, all homozygous FHM1 mutant mice (n = 7 S218L and n = 8 R192Q mutant mice) showed at least one CSD.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from CSD recordings after bone flap removal.

claim: All homozygous FHM1 mutant mice showed at least one CSD after removal of the bone flap.
source: While only one CSD was observed in 2/18 investigated WT mice (n = 8 S218L WT littermates and n = 10 R192Q WT littermates) and in 3/10 heterozygous S218L mutant mice, all homozygous FHM1 mutant mice (n = 7 S218L and n = 8 R192Q mutant mice) showed at least one CSD.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from CSD recordings after bone flap removal.

claim: Homozygous S218L mutant mice showed trains of up to four CSDs after removal of the bone flap.
source: In homozygous S218L mutant mice even trains of up to four CSDs were observed after removal of the bone flap.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from CSD recordings after bone flap removal.

claim: Mechanical stress to the dura mater alone induced CSDs in 10% of WT mice.
source: These data indicate, that mechanical stress to the dura mater alone induced CSDs in 10% of WT mice, but in 100% of homozygous FHM1 mutant mice and that heterozygous and homozygous FHM1 mutant mice had four to eight times more CSDs than WT littermate controls, respectively.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the experimental data showing 2/18 WT mice had CSDs, which is approximately 10%.

claim: Mechanical stress to the dura mater alone induced CSDs in 100% of homozygous FHM1 mutant mice.
source: These data indicate, that mechanical stress to the dura mater alone induced CSDs in 10% of WT mice, but in 100% of homozygous FHM1 mutant mice and that heterozygous and homozygous FHM1 mutant mice had four to eight times more CSDs than WT littermate controls, respectively.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data showing all homozygous FHM1 mutant mice had at least one CSD.

claim: Heterozygous and homozygous FHM1 mutant mice had four to eight times more CSDs than WT littermate controls after removal of the bone flap.
source: These data indicate, that mechanical stress to the dura mater alone induced CSDs in 10% of WT mice, but in 100% of homozygous FHM1 mutant mice and that heterozygous and homozygous FHM1 mutant mice had four to eight times more CSDs than WT littermate controls, respectively.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data comparing CSD numbers across genotypes.

claim: FHM1 mutant mice have a higher, gene-dose-dependent susceptibility to CSDs induced by mechanical stress to the dura mater as compared to their WT littermates.
source: This finding suggests that FHM1 mutant mice have a higher, gene-dose-dependent (het S218L < hom. R192Q < hom. S218L) susceptibility to CSDs induced by mechanical stress to the dura mater as compared to their WT littermates.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the experimental data showing increasing CSD numbers with gene dosage.

claim: All investigated animals generated one bihemispheric CSD immediately after the impact independent of their genotype.
source: After another 15 min of baseline recordings without further CSDs TBI was induced. All investigated animals generated one bihemispheric CSD immediately after the impact independent of their genotype as evidenced by a negative shift in the DC potential, a depression of the amplitude of the EEG signal, and a sequential increase of CBF in both hemispheres (Figure 2A) as already shown for WT mice (Figure 1D) and as previously published (von Baumgarten et al., 2008).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2A and a citation to published research (von Baumgarten et al., 2008).

claim: Only five additional CSDs were observed in the traumatized hemisphere of WT mice after the initial bihemispheric CSD.
source: After this initial bihemispheric CSD, only five additional CSDs were observed in the traumatized hemisphere of WT mice (n = 18; 0.2 CSDs/mouse/hr), findings well in line with previously published data from our laboratory (von Baumgarten et al., 2008).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data and a citation to published research (von Baumgarten et al., 2008).

claim: All FHM1 mutant mice generated numerous post-trauma CSDs.
source: In contrast, all FHM1 mutant mice generated numerous post-trauma CSDs.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data comparing CSD numbers between WT and FHM1 mutant mice.

claim: Homozygous R192Q mice generated 22 CSDs after TBI (1.5 CSDs/animal/hr).
source: In total 22, 37, and 79 CSDs (1.5, 2.5, and 7.5 CSDs/animal/hr) were observed in homozygous R192Q, heterozygous S218L, and homozygous S218L mutant mice, respectively (Figure 2B).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: Heterozygous S218L mice generated 37 CSDs after TBI (2.5 CSDs/animal/hr).
source: In total 22, 37, and 79 CSDs (1.5, 2.5, and 7.5 CSDs/animal/hr) were observed in homozygous R192Q, heterozygous S218L, and homozygous S218L mutant mice, respectively (Figure 2B).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: Homozygous S218L mice generated 79 CSDs after TBI (7.5 CSDs/animal/hr).
source: In total 22, 37, and 79 CSDs (1.5, 2.5, and 7.5 CSDs/animal/hr) were observed in homozygous R192Q, heterozygous S218L, and homozygous S218L mutant mice, respectively (Figure 2B).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: Homozygous R192Q mice generated 4 times more CSDs after TBI than WT animals.
source: Hence, homozygous R192Q, heterozygous S218L, and homozygous S218L mice generated 4, 7, and 16 times more CSDs after TBI than WT animals, respectively (p < 0.001 S218L hom. vs. S218L WT and p < 0.01 R192Q hom. vs. R192Q WT).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data with statistical analysis.

claim: Heterozygous S218L mice generated 7 times more CSDs after TBI than WT animals.
source: Hence, homozygous R192Q, heterozygous S218L, and homozygous S218L mice generated 4, 7, and 16 times more CSDs after TBI than WT animals, respectively (p < 0.001 S218L hom. vs. S218L WT and p < 0.01 R192Q hom. vs. R192Q WT).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data with statistical analysis.

claim: Homozygous S218L mice generated 16 times more CSDs after TBI than WT animals.
source: Hence, homozygous R192Q, heterozygous S218L, and homozygous S218L mice generated 4, 7, and 16 times more CSDs after TBI than WT animals, respectively (p < 0.001 S218L hom. vs. S218L WT and p < 0.01 R192Q hom. vs. R192Q WT).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data with statistical analysis.

claim: Only two bilateral CSDs were observed in WT mice later than 5 min after TBI.
source: While only two bilateral CSDs were observed in WT mice later than 5 min after TBI, 3, 9, and 29 bilateral CSDs were recorded in homozygous R192Q, heterozygous S218L, and homozygous S218L mutant mice, respectively.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from CSD recordings after TBI.

claim: 3 bilateral CSDs were recorded in homozygous R192Q mice later than 5 min after TBI.
source: While only two bilateral CSDs were observed in WT mice later than 5 min after TBI, 3, 9, and 29 bilateral CSDs were recorded in homozygous R192Q, heterozygous S218L, and homozygous S218L mutant mice, respectively.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from CSD recordings after TBI.

claim: 9 bilateral CSDs were recorded in heterozygous S218L mice later than 5 min after TBI.
source: While only two bilateral CSDs were observed in WT mice later than 5 min after TBI, 3, 9, and 29 bilateral CSDs were recorded in homozygous R192Q, heterozygous S218L, and homozygous S218L mutant mice, respectively.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from CSD recordings after TBI.

claim: 29 bilateral CSDs were recorded in homozygous S218L mice later than 5 min after TBI.
source: While only two bilateral CSDs were observed in WT mice later than 5 min after TBI, 3, 9, and 29 bilateral CSDs were recorded in homozygous R192Q, heterozygous S218L, and homozygous S218L mutant mice, respectively.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from CSD recordings after TBI.

claim: Heterozygous S218L mutant mice generated 6 CSDs in the contralateral hemisphere after TBI.
source: Heterozygous and homozygous S218L mutant mice also generated CSDs in the contralateral hemisphere (6 and 9, respectively), types of CSDs which we never observed in WT or R192Q mutant mice, the strain which carries the less severe FHM1 CaV2.1 channel mutation.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from CSD recordings after TBI.

claim: Homozygous S218L mutant mice generated 9 CSDs in the contralateral hemisphere after TBI.
source: Heterozygous and homozygous S218L mutant mice also generated CSDs in the contralateral hemisphere (6 and 9, respectively), types of CSDs which we never observed in WT or R192Q mutant mice, the strain which carries the less severe FHM1 CaV2.1 channel mutation.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from CSD recordings after TBI.

claim: Contralateral CSDs were never observed in WT or R192Q mutant mice after TBI.
source: Heterozygous and homozygous S218L mutant mice also generated CSDs in the contralateral hemisphere (6 and 9, respectively), types of CSDs which we never observed in WT or R192Q mutant mice, the strain which carries the less severe FHM1 CaV2.1 channel mutation.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from CSD recordings after TBI.

claim: FHM1 mutant mice had a gene-dose-dependent several fold higher susceptibility for post-TBI CSDs than their WT littermates.
source: Consequently, FHM1 mutant mice had a gene-dose-dependent several fold higher susceptibility for post-TBI CSDs than their WT littermates.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the experimental data showing increasing CSD numbers with gene dosage.

claim: Intermittent and synchronized EEG activity with a frequency of 4–8 Hz was observed in homozygous S218L mutant mice after TBI.
source: During the CSD and EEG recordings after TBI we observed intermittent and synchronized EEG activity with a frequency of 4–8 Hz in homozygous S218L mutant mice (Figure 3A) in parallel with tonic contraction of the tail and/or opisthotonus indicative of seizure activity.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: Homozygous S218L mutant mice showed tonic contraction of the tail and/or opisthotonus indicative of seizure activity after TBI.
source: During the CSD and EEG recordings after TBI we observed intermittent and synchronized EEG activity with a frequency of 4–8 Hz in homozygous S218L mutant mice (Figure 3A) in parallel with tonic contraction of the tail and/or opisthotonus indicative of seizure activity.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental observations during EEG recordings.

claim: Only one seizure was observed in a single WT animal after TBI.
source: While only one seizure was observed in a single WT animal, all heterozygous and homozygous S218L mutant mice had at least one seizure.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from video monitoring after TBI.

claim: All heterozygous and homozygous S218L mutant mice had at least one seizure after TBI.
source: While only one seizure was observed in a single WT animal, all heterozygous and homozygous S218L mutant mice had at least one seizure.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from video monitoring after TBI.

claim: Heterozygous S218L mutant mice had 1.0 ± 1.3 seizures after TBI.
source: Some seizures (1.0 ± 1.3) were observed in heterozygous and 2.5 ± 5.7 seizures in homozygous S218L mutant mice (Figure 3B).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: Homozygous S218L mutant mice had 2.5 ± 5.7 seizures after TBI.
source: Some seizures (1.0 ± 1.3) were observed in heterozygous and 2.5 ± 5.7 seizures in homozygous S218L mutant mice (Figure 3B).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: Seizures in affected WT mice lasted only 0.0 ± 0.4 min.
source: While seizures in affected WT mice lasted only a few seconds (0.0 ± 0.4 min; Figure 3C), the cumulative seizure duration per animal was longer in heterozygous (2.0 ± 2.5 min), and much longer in homozygous S218L mutant mice (72 ± 44 min).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: The cumulative seizure duration per animal in heterozygous S218L mutant mice was 2.0 ± 2.5 min.
source: While seizures in affected WT mice lasted only a few seconds (0.0 ± 0.4 min; Figure 3C), the cumulative seizure duration per animal was longer in heterozygous (2.0 ± 2.5 min), and much longer in homozygous S218L mutant mice (72 ± 44 min).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: The cumulative seizure duration per animal in homozygous S218L mutant mice was 72 ± 44 min.
source: While seizures in affected WT mice lasted only a few seconds (0.0 ± 0.4 min; Figure 3C), the cumulative seizure duration per animal was longer in heterozygous (2.0 ± 2.5 min), and much longer in homozygous S218L mutant mice (72 ± 44 min).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: None of the 29 investigated WT mice died during seizures after TBI.
source: While none of the 29 investigated WT mice and only one out of 28 investigated heterozygous S218L mutant mice died during seizures (3.6%), 21 out of 49 investigated homozygous S218L mutant mice (43%) died during a generalized tonic–clonic seizure after TBI.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data on mortality after TBI.

claim: Only one out of 28 investigated heterozygous S218L mutant mice died during seizures (3.6%) after TBI.
source: While none of the 29 investigated WT mice and only one out of 28 investigated heterozygous S218L mutant mice died during seizures (3.6%), 21 out of 49 investigated homozygous S218L mutant mice (43%) died during a generalized tonic–clonic seizure after TBI.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data on mortality after TBI.

claim: 21 out of 49 investigated homozygous S218L mutant mice (43%) died during a generalized tonic–clonic seizure after TBI.
source: While none of the 29 investigated WT mice and only one out of 28 investigated heterozygous S218L mutant mice died during seizures (3.6%), 21 out of 49 investigated homozygous S218L mutant mice (43%) died during a generalized tonic–clonic seizure after TBI.

claim: Unhandled WT and FHM1 mice had a normal brain water content of around 77% before TBI.
source: Unhandled WT and FHM1 mice had a normal brain water content of around 77% before TBI (Figure 4A, B – naive).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4A and 4B.

claim: Sham-operated animals had no significant brain edema formation.
source: Sham-operated animals had no significant brain edema formation, while in traumatized mice brain water content increased by 3–4% in the traumatized and by 1.5–2% in the contralateral hemisphere 24 hr after TBI (Figure 4, 4 hr after trauma, light bars), values comparable to previously published data from our laboratory (Zweckberger et al., 2006; Trabold et al., 2010).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4 and citations to published research (Zweckberger et al., 2006; Trabold et al., 2010).

claim: In traumatized mice brain water content increased by 3–4% in the traumatized hemisphere 24 hr after TBI.
source: Sham-operated animals had no significant brain edema formation, while in traumatized mice brain water content increased by 3–4% in the traumatized and by 1.5–2% in the contralateral hemisphere 24 hr after TBI (Figure 4, 4 hr after trauma, light bars), values comparable to previously published data from our laboratory (Zweckberger et al., 2006; Trabold et al., 2010).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4 and citations to published research (Zweckberger et al., 2006; Trabold et al., 2010).

claim: In traumatized mice brain water content increased by 1.5–2% in the contralateral hemisphere 24 hr after TBI.
source: Sham-operated animals had no significant brain edema formation, while in traumatized mice brain water content increased by 3–4% in the traumatized and by 1.5–2% in the contralateral hemisphere 24 hr after TBI (Figure 4, 4 hr after trauma, light bars), values comparable to previously published data from our laboratory (Zweckberger et al., 2006; Trabold et al., 2010).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4 and citations to published research (Zweckberger et al., 2006; Trabold et al., 2010).

claim: Homozygotes of both FHM1 mutant mouse lines developed significantly more severe brain edema than WT controls 24 hr after TBI.
source: Homozygotes of both FHM1 mutant mouse lines developed significantly more severe brain edema than WT controls (Figure 4A, B, 24 hr after trauma, dark bars).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4A and 4B.

claim: Brain edema formation led to an increase in ICP in all investigated groups.
source: Brain edema formation led to an increase in ICP in all investigated groups (Figure 4C).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4C.

claim: Homozygotes of both FHM1 mutant lines had a significantly more pronounced intracranial hypertension than WT mice.
source: Homozygotes of both FHM1 mutant lines had a significantly more pronounced intracranial hypertension than WT mice (Figure 4C).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4C.

claim: Homozygous S218L mutant mice showed a significantly higher lesion volume (23.0 ± 3.7 mm3) as compared to WT controls (19.0 ± 1.9 mm3) 24 hr after TBI.
source: Indeed, homozygous S218L mutant mice showed a significantly higher lesion volume (23.0 ± 3.7 mm3) as compared to WT controls 24 hr after TBI (19.0 ± 1.9 mm3; p < 0.02; Figure 5A).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5A with statistical analysis.

claim: Larger lesion volumes translated into worse neurological function in homozygous S218L mutant mice.
source: Larger lesion volumes translated into worse neurological function in homozygous S218L mutant mice (Figure 5B).
evidence: The claim is inferred from the experimental data showing correlation between lesion volume and neurological function.

claim: Homozygous S218L mutant mice showed a pronounced weight loss as a sign of a reduced physical condition.
source: In line with these findings, homozygous S218L mutant mice also showed a pronounced weigh loss as a sign of a reduced physical condition (Figure 5C).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5C.

claim: FHM1 mutant mice exhibit increased susceptibility to CSD induced by electrical stimulation.
source: FHM1 mutant mice exhibit increased susceptibility to CSD induced by electrical stimulation (van den Maagdenberg et al., 2004; van den Maagdenberg et al., 2010) or topical application of KCl to the cerebral cortex (Eikermann-Haerter et al., 2009).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published research (van den Maagdenberg et al., 2004; van den Maagdenberg et al., 2010; Eikermann-Haerter et al., 2009).

claim: FHM1 mutant mice exhibit increased susceptibility to CSD induced by topical application of KCl to the cerebral cortex.
source: FHM1 mutant mice exhibit increased susceptibility to CSD induced by electrical stimulation (van den Maagdenberg et al., 2004; van den Maagdenberg et al., 2010) or topical application of KCl to the cerebral cortex (Eikermann-Haerter et al., 2009).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to published research (Eikermann-Haerter et al., 2009).

claim: CSDs have previously been detected in TBI patients.
source: After TBI FHM1 mutant mice showed an up to 20 times higher rate of CSDs in the traumatized hemisphere, a higher seizure activity, more brain edema formation, and a worse outcome as compared to WT littermates. CSDs have previously been detected in TBI patients (Mayevsky et al., 1996; Strong et al., 2002; Fabricius et al., 2006) and in animal TBI models (Takahashi et al., 1981; Ozawa et al., 1991; Nilsson et al., 1993; von Baumgarten et al., 2008).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published research (Mayevsky et al., 1996; Strong et al., 2002; Fabricius et al., 2006).

claim: CSDs have previously been detected in animal TBI models.
source: After TBI FHM1 mutant mice showed an up to 20 times higher rate of CSDs in the traumatized hemisphere, a higher seizure activity, more brain edema formation, and a worse outcome as compared to WT littermates. CSDs have previously been detected in TBI patients (Mayevsky et al., 1996; Strong et al., 2002; Fabricius et al., 2006) and in animal TBI models (Takahashi et al., 1981; Ozawa et al., 1991; Nilsson et al., 1993; von Baumgarten et al., 2008).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published research (Takahashi et al., 1981; Ozawa et al., 1991; Nilsson et al., 1993; von Baumgarten et al., 2008).

claim: In clinical studies, more CSDs were associated with worse outcome after TBI.
source: In clinical studies, in line with the current study, more CSDs were associated with worse outcome after TBI (Lauritzen et al., 2011, Hartings et al., 2011; Chase, 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published research (Lauritzen et al., 2011, Hartings et al., 2011; Chase, 2014).

claim: CSDs may directly open the blood–brain barrier.
source: That CSDs may directly open the blood–brain barrier has been previously demonstrated (Gursoy-Ozdemir et al., 2004) and suggested for a number of neurological disorders (Takano et al., 2007; Dreier and Reiffurth, 2017; Helbok et al., 2017; Dreier et al., 2018).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published research (Gursoy-Ozdemir et al., 2004; Takano et al., 2007; Dreier and Reiffurth, 2017; Helbok et al., 2017; Dreier et al., 2018).

claim: Proposed injury mechanisms of CSDs include activation of matrix metalloproteinases.
source: Proposed injury mechanisms of CSDs include activation of matrix metalloproteinases (Gursoy-Ozdemir et al., 2004), activation of proinflammatory cytokines (Richter et al., 2017), and glutamate-mediated effects (Vinogradova, 2018; Crivellaro et al., 2021; Menyhárt et al., 2020), all of which also have been implicated in the pathophysiology of brain edema formation after TBI.
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to published research (Gursoy-Ozdemir et al., 2004).

claim: Proposed injury mechanisms of CSDs include activation of proinflammatory cytokines.
source: Proposed injury mechanisms of CSDs include activation of matrix metalloproteinases (Gursoy-Ozdemir et al., 2004), activation of proinflammatory cytokines (Richter et al., 2017), and glutamate-mediated effects (Vinogradova, 2018; Crivellaro et al., 2021; Menyhárt et al., 2020), all of which also have been implicated in the pathophysiology of brain edema formation after TBI.
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to published research (Richter et al., 2017).

claim: Proposed injury mechanisms of CSDs include glutamate-mediated effects.
source: Proposed injury mechanisms of CSDs include activation of matrix metalloproteinases (Gursoy-Ozdemir et al., 2004), activation of proinflammatory cytokines (Richter et al., 2017), and glutamate-mediated effects (Vinogradova, 2018; Crivellaro et al., 2021; Menyhárt et al., 2020), all of which also have been implicated in the pathophysiology of brain edema formation after TBI.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published research (Vinogradova, 2018; Crivellaro et al., 2021; Menyhárt et al., 2020).

claim: CSDs readily propagate into subcortical structures in FHM1 mutants, specifically in S218L mutants, with an allele-dosage effect.
source: Such a scenario is supported by previous experiments showing that CSDs readily propagate into subcortical structures in FHM1 mutants, specifically in S218L mutants, with an allele-dosage effect (Eikermann-Haerter et al., 2011) and by a study showing by diffusion weighted MRI that CSDs migrate into subcortical striatal and hippocampal regions in the same strain of mice (Cain et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published research (Eikermann-Haerter et al., 2011; Cain et al., 2017).

claim: CSDs migrate into subcortical striatal and hippocampal regions in S218L mutant mice.
source: Such a scenario is supported by previous experiments showing that CSDs readily propagate into subcortical structures in FHM1 mutants, specifically in S218L mutants, with an allele-dosage effect (Eikermann-Haerter et al., 2011) and by a study showing by diffusion weighted MRI that CSDs migrate into subcortical striatal and hippocampal regions in the same strain of mice (Cain et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to published research (Cain et al., 2017).

claim: In homozygous S218L mutant mice, seizure-related spreading depolarization in the brainstem correlated with respiratory arrest that was followed by cardiac arrest and death.
source: In fact, it was shown recently that in homozygous S218L mutant mice, seizure-related spreading depolarization in the brainstem correlated with respiratory arrest that was followed by cardiac arrest and death (Loonen et al., 2019).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to published research (Loonen et al., 2019).

claim: Spreading depolarizations during spontaneous fatal seizures invaded the respiratory centers of the brainstem to cause apnea.

claim: FHM1 mutant mice have more severe brain edema after TBI as compared with their WT littermates.
source: In conclusion, we demonstrate that FHM1 mutant mice have more severe brain edema and worse outcome after TBI as compared with their WT littermates and that this phenotype is associated with a significant and gene-dose-dependent increase in the number of postinjury CSDs.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from brain water content measurements.

claim: FHM1 mutant mice have worse outcome after TBI as compared with their WT littermates.
source: In conclusion, we demonstrate that FHM1 mutant mice have more severe brain edema and worse outcome after TBI as compared with their WT littermates and that this phenotype is associated with a significant and gene-dose-dependent increase in the number of postinjury CSDs.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from neurological outcome assessments.

claim: The worse outcome phenotype in FHM1 mutant mice is associated with a significant and gene-dose-dependent increase in the number of postinjury CSDs.
source: In conclusion, we demonstrate that FHM1 mutant mice have more severe brain edema and worse outcome after TBI as compared with their WT littermates and that this phenotype is associated with a significant and gene-dose-dependent increase in the number of postinjury CSDs.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the experimental data showing correlation between CSD numbers and outcome measures.

claim: An increased susceptibility to CSDs is a likely mechanism underlying the unfavorable outcome of FHM1 mutant mice following head injury.
source: Hence, we suggest that an increased susceptibility to CSDs is a likely mechanism underlying the unfavorable outcome of FHM1 mutant mice and FHM1 patients following head injury.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the experimental data showing correlation between CSD susceptibility and outcome.

claim: An increased susceptibility to CSDs is a likely mechanism underlying the unfavorable outcome of FHM1 patients following head injury.
source: Hence, we suggest that an increased susceptibility to CSDs is a likely mechanism underlying the unfavorable outcome of FHM1 mutant mice and FHM1 patients following head injury.
evidence: The claim is speculative, extrapolating from mouse data to human patients.

claim: Post-trauma CSDs may induce brain edema formation more directly than previously envisaged, that is without affecting CBF.
source: Furthermore, our results suggest that post-trauma CSDs may induce brain edema formation more directly than previously envisaged, that is without affecting CBF.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the experimental data showing brain edema formation despite hyperemic CBF responses.

claim: No major differences were observed between male and female animals.
source: No major differences were observed between male and female animals (data not shown).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data comparing male and female animals.

claim: Homozygous S218L mutant mice had a substantially higher mortality after TBI.
source: After TBI, all mutant mice displayed considerably more CSDs and seizures than WT mice, while S218L mutant mice had a substantially higher mortality.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data on mortality rates after TBI.

claim: CSD is the electrophysiological correlate of the migraine aura.
source: Since CSD is the electrophysiological correlate of the migraine aura, these findings corroborate the phenotype of FHM1 in humans, that is attacks of migraine with aura after mechanical stress to the brain.
evidence: The claim draws from established scientific knowledge about the relationship between CSD and migraine aura.

claim: In FHM1 mutant mice post-trauma CSDs may reach deeper brain structures like the corpus callosum or the striatum.
source: Since CSDs may theoretically cross to the opposite side of the brain only through brain structures connecting both hemispheres, our results suggest that in FHM1 mutant mice post-trauma CSDs may reach deeper brain structures like the corpus callosum or the striatum.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the observation of contralateral CSDs and knowledge of brain anatomy.

claim: Subcortical propagation of spreading depolarizations into deeper brain regions was proposed as an explanation for how CSDs may increase post-trauma mortality in FHM1 mutants.
source: Subcortical propagation of spreading depolarizations into deeper brain regions, even into thalamus in the case of homozygous S218L mutant mice, was proposed as an explanation for how CSDs may increase post-trauma mortality in FHM1 mutants.
evidence: The claim is speculative, proposing a mechanism based on inference from the data.
